extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of literary criticism (poetry readers, critics, teachers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for close reading and practical criticism of poetry: diagnosing meaning, functions of language, prosody, aesthetic vocabulary, and how subjective taste and intention affect judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish explainable from inexplicable aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: What can be explained about poetry can be separated from what cannot; explanation can help us understand poetry in general and particular passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some aspects (the 'leaning of the will' by which we choose) may remain beyond foreseeable explanation, but this should not deter critical inquiry—explanation remains useful for many points of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize subjectivity and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of opinion or taste may arise from misunderstanding of meaning or from differences in temperament and interests; such differences will persist across individuals and phases of personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit persistent disagreements without assuming moral or intellectual equivalence; subjectivity does not eliminate the question of better or worse — rather it reframes value as relative to varying states and orders of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate humility and resistance to fashionable judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Be less impressionable, less dogmatic and less uncharitable by studying others' opinions: this steadies and composes judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use study of contemporary judgments to avoid being swayed by confident or trenchant expressions; avoid regarding literary judgment as a social ordeal that forces conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat critical reading as a disciplined exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical reading of poetry is an arduous discipline that reveals the limitations under which we suffer and at the same time extends our capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use critical reading to exercise the power of choice and to order oneself; it is a means to become less imposed upon by peers and fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the four functions of language (sense, feeling, tone, intention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language in poetry operates via multiple functions: Function 1 (sense), Function 2 (feeling), Function 3 (tone), and Function 4 (intention); these may be primitive or later developments and often interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly identify which function predominates in a passage; understand that feeling and tone may be more primitive, that sense can be subordinated or abrogated, and that intention may govern relations among the functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect abrogation and subordination of sense
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry sense may be completely abrogated (e.g., ritual phrases, refrains) or subordinated to evoke feelings such that literal sense becomes negligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hastily condemn so-called 'meaningless' refrains—abrogation/subordination can be appropriate poetic devices. Recognize when sense is not meant to be examined further but to produce feeling or tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate stating feelings from presenting them
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a big difference between controlling and conveying feelings and merely talking about or stating them; conscious description of feelings is suspicious in poetry unless they are properly presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware poets who merely describe or analyse feelings (anecdotal or intellectual emotionalism). Effective poetry finds a natural form of utterance to express rather than state feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret authorial intention via form and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Intention often lies in the form, construction, development and ordering of a work and may have significance not reducible to sense, feeling or tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how order, prominence and structure produce effects (false trails, misleading hopes); intention controls the relations among sense, feeling and tone and must be apprehended by noting precedence and alternation among them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to precedence and interaction of sense, feeling, and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether we proceed from sense to feeling, vice versa, or simultaneously can make a prodigious difference in effect, altering total meaning and even the sound of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read passages with sensitivity to shifts in precedence (e.g., a verse that is 'serious' vs 'extravagant'); misreading these relations produces very different apprehensions of meaning and form (examples: Poem 1, Poem 6, Poem 11 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use aesthetic ('projectile') adjectives with linguistic caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic adjectives (beauty, pretty, pleasant, sublime, holy, etc.) carry multiple functions: they may stand for inherent properties, emotive classifications, or express the speaker's feeling, often simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which use is operative in context; avoid the Ultraquistic Subterfuge (confusion arising from projecting feelings into objects). Recognize degrees of projection (pleasant → pretty → beautiful) and the resulting ambiguities in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simplistic doctrines of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Common views of beauty range from naive objectivism through pure subjectivism to elaborate reconstructed doctrines; none provide a universally useful account for discriminating particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer pragmatic, functional accounts (e.g., 'having properties such that it arouses tendencies to self-completion in the mind') while accepting that no general account will let us inspect a set of common perceptible properties in beautiful things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study rhythm/prosody in relation to meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm is a psychological impression of proportion between durations of events, and in poetry its attribution often depends on meaning; the relation of rhythm to meaning is the central interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not study rhythm apart from meaning; be wary of prosodic description divorced from psychological relations. Prosody can be useful to indicate to others how verses may be read, but measuring rhythm separately from meaning is of doubtful value and limited scientific utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limitations and practical uses of prosody
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosodists can supply descriptions of rhythm, but such descriptions may not assist much in understanding poetically interesting examples; prosody's chief practical function is to indicate reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prosodic notation sparingly and primarily to suggest reading; accept that mechanical descriptions may be overtaken by recorded or broadcast performances (wireless, gramophone).
